summary: This note is a Wikipedia-style overview of Harvard University, covering its high rankings across several league tables, its organization into academic units and campuses in the Boston area, its large endowment, and its founding and historical development. It traces Harvard from its 1636 creation by the Massachusetts Bay Colony through secularization, the Eliot-era transformation into a research university, and the 1977 merger with Radcliffe College.
one_line: Overview of Harvard University's rankings, campuses, endowment, and history from its 1636 founding to coeducation in 1977.
key_facts: Harvard has consistently topped the Academic Ranking of World Universities (ARWU) since 2003.
Harvard has topped the THE World Reputation Rankings since 2011, the year such league tables were first published.
Harvard topped the University Ranking by Academic Performance (URAP) in 2014.
Harvard was ranked 8th on the 2013-2014 PayScale College Salary Report and 14th on the 2013 PayScale College Education Value Rankings.
In 2011, the Mines ParisTech Professional Ranking World Universities ranked Harvard 1st in the world for number of alumni holding CEO positions in Fortune Global 500 companies.
The University is organized into eleven separate academic units, ten faculties and the Radcliffe Institute for Advanced Study.
Harvard's 209-acre (85 ha) main campus is centered on Harvard Yard in Cambridge, approximately 3 miles (5 km) northwest of Boston.
Harvard's $37.6 billion financial endowment is the largest of any academic institution.
Harvard was formed in 1636 by vote of the Great and General Court of the Massachusetts Bay Colony.
In 1638, the college became home to North America's first known printing press, carried by the ship John of London.
In 1639, the college was renamed Harvard College after deceased clergyman John Harvard, an alumnus of the University of Cambridge who left the school £779 and some 400 books.
The charter creating the Harvard Corporation was granted in 1650.
Harvard is the United States' oldest institution of higher learning.
President Charles W. Eliot's tenure (1869–1909) transformed the college and affiliated professional schools into a modern research university.
Harvard was a founding member of the Association of American Universities in 1900.
The undergraduate college became coeducational after its 1977 merger with Radcliffe College.
